newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. seen facing November deadline on Food Stamps.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. seen facing November deadline on Food Stamps.

text.p: New York state, whose welfare task force decided to keep meeting until mid-October, must decide by late November whether to ask for a waiver for its Food Stamps program, a non-profit group said on Tuesday.

While 11 states already have submitted their welfare plans to Washington, according to published reports, New York still is grappling with how its program will be affected by the dramatic changes imposed by the new federal welfare reforms.

Gov. George Pataki, who has said he was concerned that the state might become even more of a magnet for the poor if its plan is too generous, has been planing to call the legislature back after the November 5 polls to approve a new program.

While the governor's task force had hoped to make its recommendations by early to mid-October, the complexity of the new federal welfare bill has delayed its work, explained John Signor, a state budget official.
One of the key issues that faces the state is the mix of federal, state and local dollars that now pay for its welfare program and how best to adjust this mix.
"I think that's something the task force is looking at, what program do we primarily use state dollars for, what program do we use federal dollars for, and is that the best way to go," said Signor.

The new federal Food Stamps program, which is paid for by Washington, only lets able-bodied individuals who do not have children collect these benefits for three months in any three-year period, unless they work part-time.

States have until November 22 to ask for waivers, which can be fairly broad or target key areas, where there are a number of recipients or a lot of people competing for jobs, for example, said Rus Sykes. He is the deputy director of the State Coummunity Aid Association in Albany.

Obtaining either type of waiver would ensure that the federal government continues paying for Food Stamps, possibly giving New York more freedom to change other programs it provides or to which it contributes.
"If you're going to tinker with cash assistance for any single and childless couples, you may not want to jeopardize any Food Stamp benefits," Sykes said.

The state's constitution obliges it to aid and care for the needy, which is one of the reasons, along with its large population of immigrants, whose benefits are being curtailed, that New York could be hit hard under the new federal plan.
Pataki, who proposed limiting the state's Home Relief program to 90 days in the 1997 budget, has said he is revisiting this possibility though the legislature did reject it.

Speculation already has begun that if the governor and legislature approve a welfare plan that is considered too draconian, it soon would face a court fight due to the state's constitutional protection for the needy in Article 17.

"If the state makes any effort to challenge Article 17 in terms of not providing for our poor and handicapped...you'll see a number of groups poised to challenge it in court," said Aaron Dare, president of the Urban League of Albany. The non-profit group seeks to train and help poor people find jobs.
New York has to submit its welfare plan by July 1997 but stands to capture a windfall of as much as $120 million, depending on how ahead it is of the summer deadline.
"I think really that Food Stamps issue is obviously the most critical issue coming up...and whether the state is going to opt in early to maximize block grant dollars," Sykes said.

Pataki has predicted that New York will meet the new work requirements, which oblige states to have 25 percent of the people who collect welfare working or enrolled in a work program during the first year. The state expects this will enable it to maximize a $2.4 billlion block grant.
